repos.name: luci-app-ps5block
repos.description: OpenWrt/LuCI app that blocks PlayStation 5 system software updates (DNS, DoT/DoH, L3) while games, PSN and other devices keep working. podkop/zapret aware.
repos.readme:
# luci-app-ps5block — PS5 system update blocker for OpenWrt

[![Release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/dyadf/luci-app-ps5block)](https://github.com/dyadf/luci-app-ps5block/releases/latest) [![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-blue.svg)](LICENSE) ![OpenWrt 22.03+](https://img.shields.io/badge/OpenWrt-22.03%2B%20(fw4)-00b5e2)

[Русская версия](README.ru.md)

An OpenWrt package with a LuCI web interface that stops a PlayStation 5 from downloading and installing system software updates. **Games, patches, PSN, the store and every other device on the network keep working.**

- One-click on/off in LuCI (**Services → PS5 Update Block**).
- Automatic console detection by MAC vendor (Sony Interactive Entertainment) and device name. If several consoles are found, LuCI lists them all and any of them can be excluded.
- Two modes: **consoles only** (by MAC) or **whole network**.
- Detailed status: which protection layers are active, drop counters, a DNS check run on the router itself.
- Aware of **podkop** and **zapret/zapret2**: the rules run before them, so update traffic cannot be carried around the block through a proxy.
- Built-in console setup guide.
- One package: `.ipk` for opkg (OpenWrt 22.03–24.10) and `.apk` for apk (OpenWrt 25.x and later).

## How it works

The block has several layers. Each one closes a different way around it:

| # | Layer | What it does | What it stops |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | DNS block | dnsmasq answers "no such domain" for `*.ps5.update.playstation.net` | the normal lookup of the update server |
| 2 | DNS redirect | every DNS request from the console (port 53, any server, IPv4/IPv6) is answered by the router | manual DNS on the console (8.8.8.8 etc.) |
| 3 | Strict DNS | external DNS is dropped **before** podkop | podkop routing the console completely and intercepting its DNS |
| 4 | DoT / DoQ | port 853 is dropped | encrypted DNS |
| 5 | DoH | ~90 addresses of public DNS/DoH resolvers are dropped (Cloudflare, Google, Quad9, AdGuard, Yandex, OpenDNS, NextDNS, …) | DNS over HTTPS |
| 6 | L3 | update server IP addresses are dropped; the router resolves them itself and refreshes the list on a schedule | a console that already knows the server IP |

All rules (except the dnsmasq entry) live in a dedicated nftables table `inet ps5block` at priority **−170**. That is before podkop's mangle chain (−150) and before zapret's queues, so a dropped packet never reaches them. Restarting the firewall, podkop or zapret does not touch the table.

```
packet from console ──► ps5block (−170): DoT / DoH / L3 / strict DNS ── drop
                              │
                              ▼
                     podkop mangle (−150) ──► NAT (−100): DNS redirect to dnsmasq
                              │                                 │
                              ▼                                 ▼
                   forward / zapret / WAN           dnsmasq: NXDOMAIN for the update domain
```

Only `ps5.update.playstation.net` and its subdomains are blocked; that is system software. Games and patches come from other domains and keep working.

## What to block

The DNS layer has three presets (**Advanced → "What to block"**, or `option blocklist`):

| Preset | Blocks | Games / store / PSN |
|---|---|---|
| **updates** (default) | system software update servers only (`update.playstation.net` + the Akamai update CDN) | keep working |
| **all** | every PlayStation/PSN server — downloads (incl. games), store, sign-in, community, STUN, APIs, `ribob01.net`, … | cut off |
| **custom** | only the domains you add under "Extra blocked domains" | — |

The preset lists live in `/usr/share/ps5block/domains.updates` and `domains.all`; "Extra blocked domains" are added on top (for **custom**, they are the whole list). The IP-level (L3) layer always targets update servers only.

## Requirements

- OpenWrt **22.03 or later** with firewall4 (nftables). This is the default since 22.03 and is also required by podkop and zapret2.
- LuCI.
- dnsmasq (the default OpenWrt DNS server; `dnsmasq-full` works too).

## Installation

The packages are signed with the project key (not the OpenWrt key). The public keys are in [`keys/`](keys/) and attached to every [release](https://github.com/dyadf/luci-app-ps5block/releases).

### Option 1: package feed (recommended, updates through opkg/apk)

**OpenWrt 22.03–24.10 (opkg):**

```sh
wget -O /etc/opkg/keys/eec9661fb33aa0db https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dyadf/luci-app-ps5block/main/keys/eec9661fb33aa0db
echo "src/gz ps5block https://github.com/dyadf/luci-app-ps5block/releases/latest/download" >> /etc/opkg/customfeeds.conf
opkg update && opkg install luci-app-ps5block
```

**OpenWrt 25.x and later (apk):**

```sh
wget -O /etc/apk/keys/ps5block.pem https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dyadf/luci-app-ps5block/main/keys/ps5block.pem
echo "https://github.com/dyadf/luci-app-ps5block/releases/latest/download/packages.adb" >> /etc/apk/repositories.d/customfeeds.list
apk update && apk add luci-app-ps5block
```

The signature is checked on every `opkg update` / `apk update`; without the key the package does not install. To update: `opkg upgrade luci-app-ps5block` or `apk upgrade luci-app-ps5block`.

### Option 2: package file by hand

Download the `.ipk` or `.apk` from the [releases page](https://github.com/dyadf/luci-app-ps5block/releases) and copy it to the router (`-O` is needed when the router has no sftp server):

```sh
scp -O luci-app-ps5block_1.5.0-r1_all.ipk root@192.168.1.1:/tmp/   # OpenWrt 22.03–24.10
scp -O luci-app-ps5block-1.5.0-r1.apk     root@192.168.1.1:/tmp/   # OpenWrt 25.x and later
```

On the router:

```sh
# OpenWrt 22.03–24.10 (opkg)
opkg install /tmp/luci-app-ps5block_1.5.0-r1_all.ipk

# OpenWrt 25.x and later (apk): with the key from keys/ in /etc/apk/keys/ the
# signature is checked, without it --allow-untrusted is needed
apk add /tmp/luci-app-ps5block-1.5.0-r1.apk
```

File checksums are in `SHA256SUMS` in the release.

Reload LuCI and open **Services → PS5 Update Block**. The package installs **disabled**, unless traces of the older scripts are found; then protection stays on (see "Migrating from the old scripts").

## First start

1. Turn the console on so it gets an address from the router.
2. In LuCI press **"Enable blocking"**.
3. The console appears in the list as **"Blocked"**. A PS5 has different MAC addresses for cable and Wi-Fi; both are detected once the console has used them.
4. Check "Protection layers": every enabled layer should be "Active", and the DNS check should say "update domain does not resolve".

### Console setup

The same guide is at the bottom of the LuCI page.

1. **DNS "Automatic":** Settings → Network → Settings → Set Up Internet Connection → your network → Advanced Settings → DNS Settings: Automatic. Manual DNS is redirected too, but "Automatic" is the most reliable, especially with podkop.
2. **Turn off automatic updates:** Settings → System → System Software → System Software Update and Settings → turn off "Download Update Files Automatically" and "Install Update Files Automatically".
3. **Delete an update that was already downloaded.** The router cannot remove what is already on the console.
4. **Power the console off completely and on again** (not rest mode) so it forgets cached DNS answers.
5. **Check:** … → Update System Software → Update Using Internet. The console must report an error instead of finding a new version.

## Modes

| Setting | Consoles only (default) | Whole network |
|---|---|---|
| Applies to | PlayStation consoles only (by MAC) | every client of the selected networks |
| DNS block | on | on |
| DNS redirect | on | on |
| Strict DNS | auto (only for consoles podkop routes completely) | off |
| DoT / DoQ | on | off |
| DoH | on | off |
| L3 (server IPs) | on | off |

In "Whole network" mode the layers that could affect other devices are off by default. They can be turned on in the "Protection layers" tab.

**When to use "Whole network":** when the console cannot be recognised by MAC (for example, MAC randomisation is on) or when you want a block without exceptions.

## Several consoles

When more than one console is found, LuCI shows a warning and lists them all. With auto-detection on, all of them are blocked. To let a console update, press **"Exclude"** next to it. A console that is not detected can be added under "Consoles added by hand".

## Sending payloads

Independently of the update block, the router can send a homebrew **payload** to a console on the LAN. Next to each console in the status list there is a **"Send payload"** button: pick an ELF/bin file and the router streams it to the console over TCP on port **9021** (configurable under **Advanced → "Payload port"**).

- The console must already be running a payload loader that listens on that port (set up on the console itself, from its browser/exploit entry point). This package does not exploit or modify the console; it only transfers a file you provide to a loader that is already listening.
- The uploaded file lives only in the router's RAM (`/tmp/ps5block-payload/`) and is **deleted right after it is sent**, whether the send succeeds or fails.
- **The port is checked automatically before sending.** The payload is transmitted to the console only if its loader is listening on the port; otherwise nothing is sent and the uploaded file is removed. You can also check on demand with the **"Check port"** button or `ps5block payload-check <MAC|IP>` (open / closed / no IP).
- A loader that accepts only a **single** connection would spend it on the automatic check. For such a loader, send from the command line with the check disabled: `PS5BLOCK_SKIP_PORTCHECK=1 ps5block payload <MAC|IP> <file>`.
- From the command line: `ps5block payload <MAC|IP> <file>` (the file must be in `/tmp/ps5block-payload/`).

This is meant for your own console on your own network.

## podkop, zapret and DoH

- **podkop.** Compatible, including podkop's own DNS handling. podkop (and fw4/AdGuard) redirect LAN DNS at NAT priority −100; this package redirects the console's DNS at −160, so it **claims the console's queries first** and they always reach dnsmasq — the DNS block is not bypassed even when podkop owns port 53. This covers "Automatic" DNS on the console too (all of its port-53 traffic is caught, not only queries to external servers). The DoT/DoH/L3 drops run at −170, before podkop's −150, so update traffic never reaches the proxy. Only the console is affected; other clients keep using podkop's DNS. When the podkop list changes, the rules rebuild themselves on the next refresh (every 20 minutes by default) or at once with "Re-apply rules". **Do not put playstation domains into podkop lists**; the package warns if it finds them.
- **zapret / zapret2.** Compatible. zapret works on outgoing WAN traffic, and dropped packets never get there.
- **DoH on the router (https-dns-proxy etc.).** Compatible: it is dnsmasq's upstream, and the dnsmasq entry answers first.
- **AdGuard Home.** If it replaces dnsmasq on port 53, the DNS layer does not work: add `||ps5.update.playstation.net^` to its blocklist. All other layers keep working.

## Forcing the console's DNS

By default the console's DNS is redirected to the router's dnsmasq (that is how the DNS block works); only the console's DNS aimed at **external** servers is redirected, so "Automatic" DNS on the console keeps working through the router and general internet is never broken.

To make the console use **specific** resolver(s) instead, set **Protection layers → "Force DNS to this server"** (`list dns_server`) — one or more IPs. The console's port-53 queries are directed to a dedicated local forwarder that resolves via those server(s), overriding podkop/AdGuard; with several, queries are spread across them. Queries for blocked update domains are still intercepted and blocked by the router. **Make sure the servers are reachable — a dead server here means no DNS for the console.** (The "Resolvers" field is unrelated — it only tells the router which DNS to use when looking up the update servers' IPs for the L3 layer.)

## Command line

```sh
ps5block status          # detailed status
ps5block enable|disable  # turn on / off
ps5block mode mac|global # mode
ps5block detect          # detected consoles
ps5block add AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF "PS5 living room"  # add by hand
ps5block exclude AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF                # exclude a console
ps5block remove AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF                 # forget a hand-added console
ps5block refresh         # refresh update server IPs and consoles
ps5block ruleset         # print the nftables rules that would be loaded
ps5block payload AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF payload.bin   # send /tmp/ps5block-payload/payload.bin, then delete it
ps5block payloads        # list uploaded payloads waiting to be sent (JSON)
ps5block payload-check AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF          # is the console listening on the payload port? (JSON)
```

Settings live in `/etc/config/ps5block`; logs: `logread -e ps5block`.

## Migrating from the old scripts

On installation the package cleans up after the earlier scripts:

- **`ps5_update_block.sh`** (pureair): 41 dnsmasq entries, including `gs2.ww.prod.dl…` and `sgst.prod.dl…`, which most likely also blocked game downloads.
- **`ps5block.sh`** (stand-alone script): `ps5blk_*` firewall rules, include, cron, `/etc/ps5block.conf`.

Your own dnsmasq entries, firewall rules and cron jobs are not touched. If the old block was active, the package starts enabled and carries the console MAC addresses over, so protection is never interrupted.

## Removal

```sh
opkg remove luci-app-ps5block   # or: apk del luci-app-ps5block
```

Removal deletes the nftables table, the dnsmasq entry and the cron job. `/etc/config/ps5block` stays; delete it by hand if you no longer need it.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | What to check |
|---|---|
| Console not listed | It must get its address from this router. Run `ps5block detect`. If it is missing, add the MAC by hand (PS5: Settings → System → System Software → Console Information). |
| A layer says "Not loaded" | Press "Re-apply rules" and read the nftables error on the page or in `logread -e ps5block`. |
| "update domain still resolves" | DNS is not served by dnsmasq (e.g. AdGuard Home), or the entry was removed by hand. Press "Re-apply rules". |
| The console still found an update | It was downloaded earlier (delete it on the console); the console is on another network; the console is not in the blocked list. |
| Something other than updates breaks | Turn off L3 in "Protection layers": CDN addresses are shared with other services. |

## Limitations

The router only controls its own network. A console connected to another network (phone hotspot, another router), or updated from a USB drive, is not covered. Sony may change the update domains; the domain list can be edited in LuCI ("Advanced" tab).

## Building from source

```sh
# quick .ipk and .apk build without the SDK → dist/
PO2LMO=/path/to/po2lmo APK=/path/to/apk ./build.sh

# signed: .apk + packages.adb (EC P-256) and Packages.sig for opkg (usign)
PO2LMO=... APK=... APK_KEY=~/keys/apk-private.pem \
  USIGN=/path/to/usign USIGN_KEY=~/keys/usign.sec ./build.sh

# or in the OpenWrt SDK: put the directory into feeds/luci/applications/
make package/luci-app-ps5block/compile
```

`po2lmo` is built from `luci/modules/luci-base/src`, `apk` from apk-tools 3.x, `usign` from `git.openwrt.org/project/usign`. The version comes from the `Makefile` (`PKG_VERSION`, `PKG_RELEASE`). Private keys never go into the repository (`.gitignore`); the public keys are in `keys/`.

## Tests

```sh
# backend: busybox ash + the real uci/jshn/jsonfilter (built for the host) + the real nft
# in a private user/network namespace; the host is not touched
JSHN=/path/to/jshn.sh PATH=/path/to/openwrt-host-tools/bin:$PATH tests/run.sh

# LuCI page: strings from the router never end up as HTML
node tests/view.test.js
```

`tests/run.sh` covers enable/disable, the nftables rules, dnsmasq, cron, the update server list, consoles, podkop, rpcd, hotplug, migration from the old scripts and live traffic through a bridge with a "console" and a "phone" (158 checks).

The package was also tested in an emulated OpenWrt environment: busybox ash, the real `uci`, `jshn`, `jsonfilter`, `opkg` and `apk` 3.0 built from OpenWrt sources, the real `nft` with a Linux kernel; installation, reinstallation and removal with opkg and apk, installation from the signed apk feed; rendering of the LuCI page in English and Russian.

**It has not been run on a physical router yet.** If something goes wrong, please open an [issue](https://github.com/dyadf/luci-app-ps5block/issues) with the output of `ps5block status` and `logread -e ps5block`.

## Contributors

See [CONTRIBUTORS.md](CONTRIBUTORS.md). Changes are listed in [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md).

## License

[MIT](LICENSE) © 2026 arsutov and contributors.

The MAC prefix list (`oui.txt`) is taken from the public IEEE MA-L registry and the DNS resolver addresses from their operators' public documentation; both are factual data. LuCI, OpenWrt, podkop and zapret are separate projects under their own licenses; none of their code is included. PlayStation and PS5 are trademarks of Sony Interactive Entertainment; this project is not affiliated with Sony.

latestRelease.name: v1.5.1 — preserve DNS block with custom Force-DNS resolver
latestRelease.body:
### Fixed
- **DNS blocking preserved when "Force DNS to this server" (`dns_server`) is configured.** Previously, pointing `dns_server` to an external resolver bypassed the router's DNS block rules via direct DNAT, leaving DNS blocking inactive on the console.
  `ps5block` now launches an isolated, lightweight local dnsmasq forwarder on port 5553 whenever custom `dns_server` entries are configured. The forwarder serves the active blocklists (update servers, presets, and custom domains) directly as NXDOMAIN, while forwarding allowed queries to the specified upstream server(s). Redirect rules in nftables send console port-53 queries to this dedicated forwarder, preserving full DNS blocking while honoring the chosen DNS server.

> ⚠️ Private/unstable. Tested in emulation (busybox, real uci/jshn/jsonfilter/nft/apk, live traffic through a bridge). 160 checks.

See [CHANGELOG.md](https://github.com/dyadf/luci-app-ps5block/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md).

repos.name: garlic-savemgr
repos.description: A Local Save Manager for your PS5
repos.readme:
# Garlic SaveMgr for PS5

PS5 save decrypt/encrypt/browse with embedded web UI.

## Usage

1. Send `garlic-savemgr.elf` to elfldr
2. Open `http://<ps5-ip>:8082` in your browser on your PC
3. Drag and drop files into the browse tab to add/replace files

## Cloud Backups

Open the Settings tab in the web UI to edit `/data/garlic/cloud.json`.
You can also create the file manually:

```json
{
  "enabled": true,
  "provider": "ftp",
  "watch_titles": ["PPSA01234", "CUSA12345"],
  "ftp": {
    "host": "ftp.example.com",
    "port": 21,
    "user": "username",
    "pass": "password",
    "remote_path": "/ps5-saves/",
    "use_tls": false
  },
  "auto_backup": {
    "enabled": true,
    "poll_seconds": 5,
    "settle_seconds": 15,
    "queue_for_browser_drive": true
  },
  "backup_targets": {
    "local": {
      "enabled": false,
      "path": "/data/garlic/backups"
    },
    "usb": {
      "enabled": true,
      "path": "/mnt/usb0/garlic-backups"
    },
    "ftp": {
      "enabled": true
    },
    "google_drive": {
      "enabled": false
    }
  },
  "google_drive": {
    "mode": "browser",
    "folder_id": "drive_folder_id_shared_with_service_account",
    "service_account": {
      "type": "service_account",
      "project_id": "...",
      "private_key_id": "...",
      "private_key": "-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----\n...\n-----END PRIVATE KEY-----\n",
      "client_email": "...",
      "client_id": "...",
      "auth_uri": "https://accounts.google.com/o/oauth2/auth",
      "token_uri": "https://oauth2.googleapis.com/token",
      "auth_provider_x509_cert_url": "...",
      "client_x509_cert_url": "...",
      "universe_domain": "googleapis.com"
    }
  }
}
```

The Browse tab exposes Cloud Backup actions for a selected save and for all saves under a title. Backups are encrypted/restorable ZIP archives. PS5 archives contain the raw save image; PS4 archives include the `sdimg_...` image and its `.bin` key companion when present.

Supported destinations:

- `local`: writes encrypted/restorable ZIP archives on the PS5, defaulting to `/data/garlic/backups`.
- `usb`: writes encrypted/restorable ZIP archives to a connected USB drive, defaulting to `/mnt/usb0/garlic-backups`.
- `ftp`: uploads from the PS5 to a passive plain FTP server.
- `google_drive` with `"mode": "browser"`: the browser fetches the backup ZIP from the PS5 and uploads it to Google Drive. Use service-account auth for Shared Drives, or Browser OAuth Token auth for normal personal My Drive folders.
- `google_drive` with `"mode": "direct"`: configurable, but disabled in this payload build because the PS5 SDK image exposes `libSceSsl.so` without public SSL headers for a safe HTTPS implementation.

The legacy top-level `provider` field still works, but `backup_targets` can enable multiple destinations at once. Manual and auto title backups package one encrypted/restorable ZIP under `/data/garlic/tmp`, then distribute that same ZIP to every enabled PS5-side destination (`local`, `usb`, `ftp`). Google Drive browser mode remains a browser/queue destination.

For Google Drive browser mode, the Drive folder ID is required. Folder names like `ps5_saves` are not accepted as IDs. Service accounts do not have storage quota in normal My Drive folders, so they can only upload to Shared Drives or Workspace delegated drives. For a personal My Drive folder, select Browser OAuth Token in Settings and paste a Drive-scoped access token. Settings -> Test Drive Access verifies the selected auth can see and upload to the folder.

When `auto_backup.enabled` is true, Garlic SaveMgr starts a watcher thread. It probes the PS5 LNC symbols for the running Big App title, snapshots watched save mtimes/sizes when a title starts, then waits `settle_seconds` after the title closes before backing up changed saves. If the LNC probe is unavailable, it falls back to mtime polling for watched titles.

Auto upload behavior:

- FTP uploads immediately from the PS5 using the same encrypted/restorable title ZIP as Cloud Backup All.
- Local and USB targets write immediately from the PS5 using the same encrypted/restorable title ZIP as Cloud Backup All. Files are written as `.tmp` first, then renamed to `.zip` when complete.
- Google Drive browser mode writes pending ZIPs to `/data/garlic/cloud_queue/`. The Settings page polls the queue and uploads pending backups when the browser is open with valid Drive auth.
- Google Drive direct mode remains unsupported, but can still queue browser uploads when `queue_for_browser_drive` is true.

The manual API endpoints are:

- `GET /api/settings/cloud`
- `POST /api/settings/cloud`
- `GET /api/cloud/status`
- `GET /api/cloud/upload?idx=N&mode=enc`
- `GET /api/cloud/upload_title?id=<title_id>&mode=enc`
- `GET /api/cloud/package?idx=N`
- `GET /api/cloud/package_title?id=<title_id>`
- `GET /api/cloud/auto_status`
- `POST /api/cloud/auto_scan`
- `GET /api/cloud/queue`
- `GET /api/cloud/queue_download?id=<queue_id>`
- `POST /api/cloud/queue_done?id=<queue_id>`

If `watch_titles` is non-empty, manual cloud uploads are limited to those title IDs. FTP `use_tls` still fails with a clear error instead of silently downgrading.

## Quick Setup: Local FTP Server (Windows & Docker)

If you want to test cloud backups locally without routing through a cloud service, you can spin up a temporary, isolated FTP server on your Windows PC using Docker.

This setup automatically bridges a local folder on your PC to the FTP server, so any files sent from your PS5 will instantly appear on your desktop.

### Prerequisites

1. Install [Docker Desktop for Windows](https://www.docker.com/products/docker-desktop/).
2. Ensure Docker Desktop is open and the Engine is running.
3. Open a **PowerShell** window.

### Step 1: Prepare your Workspace

First, create a folder where you want your saves to land, and navigate inside it using PowerShell:

```powershell
# Create the folder on your desktop and navigate to it
mkdir ~\Desktop\PS5_SAVES
cd ~\Desktop\PS5_SAVES
```

### Step 2: Spin up the FTP Server

Run the following command.

*Note: Replace `192.168.1.X` with your computer's actual local network IP address (you can find this by running `ipconfig` and looking for your IPv4 Address).*

```powershell
docker run -d -p 21:21 -p 21000-21010:21000-21010 `
  -e USERS="ps5_saves|password|/ftp/ps5_saves" `
  -e ADDRESS="192.168.1.X" `
  -v "${PWD}:/ftp/ps5_saves" `
  delfer/alpine-ftp-server
```

**What this does:**

* Creates an FTP user named `ps5_saves` with the password `password`.
* Locks the user into the `/ftp/ps5_saves` directory.
* Maps your current Windows folder (`${PWD}`) directly to that internal directory so files sync instantly.
* Broadcasts your real local IP (`ADDRESS`) so passive FTP connections don't time out.

### Step 3: Windows Firewall (Crucial)

By default, Windows aggressively blocks external devices from talking to Docker. To let your PS5 connect:

1. Ensure your Windows Network Profile is set to **Private**, not Public.
2. In your Windows Defender Firewall settings, allow the **Docker Desktop Backend** executable through the firewall on Private networks.

### Step 4: Configure Garlic SaveMgr

Open the web UI at `http://<ps5-ip>:8082`, go to **Settings**, and set the FTP provider (or edit `/data/garlic/cloud.json` directly):

```json
"ftp": {
  "host": "192.168.1.X",
  "port": 21,
  "user": "ps5_saves",
  "pass": "password",
  "remote_path": "/",
  "use_tls": false
}
```

Use **Test FTP** in Settings to verify connectivity, then run **Cloud Backup** (or **Cloud Backup All** on a title) from the save list. Files will drop into your Windows `PS5_SAVES` folder.

**Tear Down:**

When you are done testing, kill the background server by grabbing the container ID and forcing it to stop:

```powershell
docker ps
docker rm -f <CONTAINER_ID>
```

## Building

Requires the [PS5 Payload SDK](https://github.com/ps5-payload-dev/sdk).

```sh
make PS5_PAYLOAD_SDK=/path/to/ps5-payload-sdk
```

repos.name: kstuff-lite
repos.readme:
# kstuff-lite — `1.11-opt`

`1.11-opt` builds on the existing kstuff-lite crypto, FSELF, NPDRM, and loader
work. It reduces UELF/KELF transition cost, makes FPU/CR0 handling safer and
faster, and adds detailed opt-in diagnostics.

## Highlights

- Cached translations for fixed per-CPU kernel objects used on every UELF
  entry, including mappings that cross a physical segment boundary.
- Narrow checked trap-frame and stack reads instead of copying unused frame
  prefixes.
- A single-transition debug-register restore and skipped hardware snapshots
  when the current thread does not own active debug registers.
- A validated, normally fault-free CR0 save/TS-clear chain with mandatory
  per-kernel gadgets and no legacy CR0-capture fallback.
- Fast CR0 entry through a one-shot KELF continuation and deferred CR0 restore
  at the final KELF exit.
- Runtime selection between `XSAVEC` and `XSAVE`, with one-time CPUID/XCR0
  discovery and strict save-area validation.
- Expanded opt-in performance and failure metrics through `KSTUFF_OBS=1`.
- Reuse of the loader's existing kernel pipe by prosper0gdb.

## UELF trap and kernel-memory paths

### Narrow checked frame reads

Trap handlers now read only the portion of a saved stack frame that they use.
`fpkg`, `kekcall`, and utility trap handling use checked tail-copy helpers;
mailbox and syscall paths use checked scalar reads and writes. Where the return
address is already known, FSELF handling updates `RSP` and `RIP` directly
instead of reading the same value from kernel memory again.

This reduces `virt2phys` calls and copied bytes without weakening error
handling. A failed read or write returns `EFAULT` or leaves the request on its
normal fallback path instead of consuming partially read state.

### Fixed mapping caches

The following stable per-CPU objects have cached virtual-to-physical mappings:

- the extended trap frame;
- the `justreturn` frame;
- the current-thread pointer in `pcpu`;
- `TSS.RSP0`;
- the `wrmsr` argument area;
- the CR0 enter and exit continuation slots.

The cache can represent two physical segments, so an object crossing a page or
mapping boundary does not need to fall back on every access. Initialization is
checked, publication is atomic, and an uncached checked copy remains available
if a mapping cannot be cached.

The UELF page-table setup also spells out the user, writable, present, and
large-page flags explicitly. Direct-map entries are not made global, avoiding
unsafe stale TLB translations when switching between the kernel and UELF CR3.

## Crypto dispatch

During classification, the fake key is retrieved once and passed to the XTS or
HMAC handler. This removes the former `has_fake_key()` lookup followed by a
second `get_fake_key()` lookup. XTS and HMAC cache selection also performs one
scan that records both a matching entry and the first free entry.

Unhandled or non-fake messages retain the original kernel path, and linked
message chains are still traversed correctly. Snapshot read failures are
counted and fail safely.

## Debug-register transitions

Debug-register restore now enters the verified tail of the kernel
`cpu_switch` implementation and restores DR0, DR1, DR2, DR3, DR6, and DR7 in a
single gadget transition. Each kernel layout uses its own validated entry.

Before installing a watchpoint, the code checks `PCB_DBREGS`. If the flag is
clear, the thread does not own live hardware debug-register state, so a stale
hardware snapshot is skipped and the saved state is initialized as disabled.
PCB flags are accessed as a 32-bit field, and rollback restores both the old
registers and the original ownership flag if installation fails.

KELF 8-byte writes also use a scalar `mov [rdi], rax` store helper instead of
configuring `rep movsb` for every single-qword update.

## FPU and CR0 handling

### CR0 entry

UELF crypto uses SIMD instructions and must preserve kernel FPU state while
temporarily clearing `CR0.TS`. The entry path is a kernel-specific KELF
chain: it single-steps `mov_rax_cr0`, captures the resulting `#DB`, clears TS,
commits the new value, and records all three states without deliberately
causing a second XSAVE/FXSAVE fault. Failure to arm or validate this chain is
reported directly; there is no CR0-capture fallback.

The chain poisons and transfers one compact `0x60`-byte result block,
then validates the saved, cleared, and committed values. A mismatch restores
TS when possible and reports failure instead of trusting partial state.

### Fast entry and deferred restore

UELF arms a one-shot KELF continuation and performs one
`yield()`; KELF resets the hook before running the CR0 chain. This bypasses the
generic full-register gadget return path. The fixed continuation address and
its physical mapping are cached after the first use.

After `XRSTOR`, CR0 restoration is postponed until `uelf_fpu_finish()`, just
before the terminal UELF `HLT`. KELF then restores CR0 and continues through
the normal final exit. Nested FPU users share the outer save/restore pair, so
they do not add extra CR0 or XSAVE transitions.

### XSAVE mode selection

CPUID and XCR0 discovery is performed once per UELF instance. Before using an
architectural save instruction, the code verifies:

- CPUID exposes leaf `0xD`;
- the CPU and OS expose XSAVE/OSXSAVE;
- x87 and SSE are enabled in XCR0;
- XCR0 contains only state components reported by CPUID;
- `CPUID.(D,0):EBX` is within the architectural minimum, the reported maximum,
  and the 4096-byte aligned local buffer.

`XSAVEC` is selected when `CPUID.(D,1):EAX[1]` advertises it; otherwise the code
uses `XSAVE`. Restore always uses `XRSTOR`. `XSAVEOPT` is deliberately not used
because the scratch buffer is not guaranteed to contain the same owner's
previous state. An unusable configuration disables FPU entry cleanly instead
of overflowing the buffer or executing an unsupported instruction.

## prosper0gdb loader handoff

The loader passes prosper0gdb a versioned bootstrap structure containing its
existing read/write pipe descriptors and kernel pipe address. prosper0gdb
reuses that primitive instead of allocating and resolving another pipe. The
older `victim_pktopts` ABI remains recognized for callers that do not provide
the bootstrap magic.

## Observability

Build with metrics and the debug reader enabled:

```sh
export PS5_PAYLOAD_SDK=/opt/ps5-payload-sdk
KSTUFF_OBS=1 ./ci-ps5-kstuff-ldr.sh
```

A normal build keeps the extra counters out of hot paths:

```sh
./ci-ps5-kstuff-ldr.sh
```

The added metrics cover:

- UELF entries, checked frame failures, and total/max entry cycles;
- gadget calls, failures, result-readback reductions, and cycles;
- scalar and bulk kernel copies;
- crypto snapshot reads, failures, and cycles;
- mapping-cache hits, misses, and fallbacks;
- debug-register reads, writes, single-transition chains, and skipped
  snapshots;
- CR0 fast-entry/deferred-restore arms, failures, hook-cache use,
  and arm cost;
- FPU enter/exit, XSAVE/XSAVEC/XRSTOR counts, failures, and cycle cost;
- PLAINTEXT_NOAUTH FE/FF index acquisition and exact transient-context cleanup
  before `ppfs_put_{cmac,xts}_index` (`PPRCLN01` word-log records).

`ps5-kstuff/debug-reader.c` prints these counters from the shared observation
area. Metrics are intended for comparison runs; they add measurement overhead
and should not be used as release-performance numbers.

repos.name: ps5-app-dumper
repos.readme:
# PS5 App Dumper

**PS5 App Dumper**

A small utility to dump PS5 application files from the console's `pfsmnt` to a connected USB storage device. This project builds into an ELF payload that runs on the PS5 and copies the app files to a mounted USB drive — **it does not support network transfers**.

Since v1.11 the payload also serves a **web interface**. Start it once, then drive the dump from your phone or PC: pick the running title, pick the drive, change the settings and watch the progress live. The game keeps running the whole time.

---

## Important note

This tool **only dumps to USB**. The web interface controls the dump over the network, but the files themselves are always written to a drive attached to the console. It does **not** stream or transfer dumps over the network.

---

## Web interface

![Web UI](docs/webui.png)

1. Plug in the USB drive and start the payload (see *Usage* below). A notification shows the address, for example `http://192.168.1.42:8081`.
2. Open that address in any browser on the same network — a phone or PC works well, or the console's own browser.
3. Press **Start** on a title, or launch the game on the console yourself. The game that is up appears as a card at the top of the list.
4. Once it shows up under **Running**, choose the destination drive and press **Start dump**.

The page shows every mounted title with its name, icon and version, the size of the selected title against the free space on each drive, the live transfer rate with an ETA, and the full log output. Settings changed in the page are written straight to `config.ini`.

**Starting titles:** the list shows what is installed on the console, internal and external drives alike, with the running game on top. Press **Start** and the payload launches the title, waits for it to mount and selects it for you. A PS5 runs one game at a time, so starting a title closes the running one — the button asks first.

Not every title starts this way. A title that the console itself refuses to launch from the home screen will not start from here either, and the page says so. If the console does not expose the launch service at all, the tab still lists the titles but without Start buttons.

**Disc or package:** every title carries a **DISC** or **PKG** badge, and **DISC OUT** marks a disc game whose disc is not in the drive. With the disc out the payload goes by what it has seen before (kept in `disc_titles.txt` next to `config.ini`) and by the disc-copy bitmap an install from disc leaves behind — a guess, which the queue lets you correct.

**Queue:** press **+ Queue** on several installed titles (up to 64) to dump them in one go. The queue card on the right orders them, and **Start queue** hands the list to the console: each title is started — which closes the one before it — and once it shows up as the running title it gets the *load time* to finish loading (`queue_delay`, 30 seconds by default) before it is dumped. A title that does not come up, does not fit on the drive or fails to dump is marked and the queue moves on. **Stop queue** aborts the current dump and skips the rest; the button next to it leaves only the title at hand and lets the queue carry on with the next one - **Skip this title** while it waits for a disc, the launch or the load time, **Stop this dump** once it is dumping, which asks first because the files written so far stay behind incomplete.

Several disc games can share a queue. When the next title is a disc game and its disc is not in the drive, the queue holds — for as long as it takes, with a reminder on the console every two minutes — and carries on a few seconds after the disc is in. Every queued title has a settings button: decrypt, FSELF, backport target and the PS4 split mode can differ from title to title, and a title with settings of its own is marked **CUSTOM**. Each dump writes the settings it ran with into the log.

Click the DISC/PKG badge of a queued title to correct it before starting. The queue runs on the console, so the browser can be closed in the meantime.

Before a dump starts, single or queued, its size is compared with the free space on the drive; a dump that would not fit is refused instead of filling the drive.

**Already dumped:** a title with a finished dump anywhere the *Dumps* page looks carries a **DUMPED** badge, one with only a dump that was cut short **UNFINISHED**; hover it for the folder.

**Installing:** a title the console is still downloading shows **INSTALLING nn%** and cannot be dumped yet - a dump would have holes. Below 100 % for good is normal: the console only fetches the PlayGo chunks it wants (its languages and region), and such a title shows how many and is dumped as it is. Whether an install is still running is told by the install bitmap changing; the shell's PlayGo status is only trusted for which chunks are wanted, since it is not always updated after an install.

**DLC:** every title shows how many DLC are installed for it; hover the badge for their names and sizes. Most of them only unlock content that is in the game already - the console never mounts those, there is nothing to dump, and they keep working for a dump started on the same console. DLC with content of their own are mounted while the game runs and are dumped with it, each as a folder of its own next to the game's (`dump_dlc`, on by default). **Dump DLC** on the running game's card dumps them alone, next to a dump made before: with one it starts at once, with several (or one that is dumped already) a list on the card picks which; a picked DLC that is there already is replaced.

**When the payload is not running:** the PS5 browser keeps a copy of the page (HTML5 application cache), so the home-screen shortcut opens it even then. The page says that the dumper is not running and reconnects by itself once it is. If Payload Manager (pldmgr) is running on the console and has a ps5-app-dumper ELF in its payload list (any file name starting with `ps5-app-dumper`), the page offers a button that asks it to start the dumper. Nothing depends on this: without pldmgr the button simply is not there. After updating the payload the cached page refreshes itself on the next visit.

**Keeping it in Payload Manager:** a payload sent over the network is gone after a reboot. Under *Menu > Settings* the page can store the running version in pldmgr as `ps5-app-dumper_v<version>.elf`; pldmgr reads the version it shows from that file name. The build embeds a copy of the ELF for this, which is why it is built in two stages.

**Rest mode:** the payload survives it. The console switches its network off when it goes to rest, and takes the USB drives with it; the web UI waits, listens on the same port again once the network is back and says so with a notification, and the settings return to the drive when it is mounted again. Do not send the console to rest while a dump to a USB drive is running: the drive goes away under it.

**Port:** the first port tried is `8081`, because the homebrew launcher normally holds `8080`. If it is busy the payload walks up to nine ports further and announces the one it settled on. Set `web_port` in `config.ini` to pick another.

**Home-screen shortcut:** open **Menu > Settings** and press **Install** next to *Home-screen shortcut* to put an "App Dumper" tile on the console's home screen. The tile opens the web interface in the console's browser. It is a shortcut only: it does **not** start the payload, so load the payload first as usual. The tile remembers the port the web interface was using when it was installed; if that changes, press **Reinstall**. Installing is refused while a dump or a queue is running. To remove the tile, delete it from the home screen like any other title.

**Turning it off:** set `enable_webui = 0` to go back to the old behaviour (dump the running title immediately and exit). With `auto_start = 1` the payload dumps the running title right at launch *and* serves the web interface, so the dump can be watched or stopped and the switch can be turned off again.

**Access code:** anyone on your network can open the page and look, but a phone or PC has to enter a six-digit code once before it may start, stop or delete anything. The console shows the code in the notification it sends at start; the dialog that asks for it can put it on the TV again, and a device that is already in finds it under *Menu > Settings*. The console's own browser never needs it. The code is kept in `config.ini` (`access_code`, next to the `access_token` devices hold afterwards) — delete both lines to lock every device out and get a new code, or switch *Ask other devices for a code* off under *Menu > Settings* to do without (`require_code = 0`). That switch only works in the console's own browser, so a phone that got in cannot leave the door open.

> The code keeps other people's devices from *changing* things. It does not hide anything: the title list, the log and folder names on your drives are readable by anyone who can reach the console, and the connection is plain HTTP. Use it on a network you trust, and shut the payload down from the footer link when you are done.

---

## Requirements

* PS5 Payload SDK by John Tornblom (required). Download and install the SDK and make it available at build time (example: `/opt/ps5-payload-sdk`).

  * Repository: [https://github.com/ps5-payload-dev/pacbrew-repo](https://github.com/ps5-payload-dev/pacbrew-repo)

* A PS5 able to run payloads (Jailbroken 1.00 - 13.60).

  * The web interface and what came with it - starting titles, the home-screen shortcut, replacing a running copy - have been tested on firmware **5.10** and **12.00**. They go through system services that differ between firmwares, so other versions may behave differently; the dump itself does not depend on them.

* A USB drive formatted and mounted on the PS5 (the dumper writes files to the USB).

* **elfldr.elf** — all delivery methods require `elfldr.elf` running on the PS5 to accept and execute incoming payloads. Download: [https://github.com/ps5-payload-dev/elfldr/releases/tag/v0.21](https://github.com/ps5-payload-dev/elfldr/releases/tag/v0.21)

---

## Building

1. Download and install the required PS5 Payload SDK. Note its path (we'll use `/opt/ps5-payload-sdk` as an example).

2. Point the project at the SDK by exporting the environment variable or editing the `Makefile`:

```bash
export PS5_PAYLOAD_SDK=/opt/ps5-payload-sdk
```

3. Build from the repository root:

```bash
make
```

You should get an ELF binary such as `ps5-app-dumper.elf`.

The web console stands on **webhb**, the web-homebrew core that grew in this repository and is a project of its own now. It is not copied in here: `webhb.lock` pins a release (version, download URL, sha256), and the first `make` installs exactly that archive into `ext/webhb/` (`tools/get-webhb.sh`). With a webhb checkout next to this repository (`../webhb`) and nothing installed, the checkout is used instead; `make WEBHB_DIR=<path>` points anywhere else, `WEBHB_TARBALL=<file> tools/get-webhb.sh` installs from a local archive.

---

### Working on it without a console

`harness/` builds the web server, the dump job, the queue and the dump store for the host and runs them against a pretend console: `make -C harness run`, then open `http://127.0.0.1:8099/`. It needs no SDK. `make -C harness snapshot` records every route's answer and `make -C harness styles` the computed style of every element in every view - two ways to show that a change which was not meant to be seen cannot be seen. See `harness/README.md` for what it can and cannot show.

## Usage

Every method needs the USB drive **plugged into the console**. With the web interface the game can be started after the payload; in headless mode (`enable_webui = 0`) the game has to be **running already** when the payload launches.

### Method 1 — Homebrew launcher + webserv

1. **Copy `ps5-app-dumper` folder** to:

   * `/data/homebrew/`
   * `/mnt/usb#/homebrew/` *(replace `#` with your USB number, e.g., `usb0`, `usb1`, etc.)*
   * `/mnt/ext#/homebrew/` *(replace `#` with your EXT number, e.g., `ext0`, `ext1`, etc.)*

2. **Included Payload Files:**

   * `ps5-app-dumper.elf`
   * `homebrew.js`

3. Open the Homebrew Launcher with webserv loaded. You will see **PS5 App Dumper** listed. Select it — the payload starts in the background and shows the address of its web interface as a notification.

**Downloads:**

* Homebrew launcher: [https://github.com/ps5-payload-dev/websrv/releases/tag/v0.24](https://github.com/ps5-payload-dev/websrv/releases/tag/v0.24)
* webserv: [https://github.com/ps5-payload-dev/websrv/releases/tag/v0.26.1](https://github.com/ps5-payload-dev/websrv/releases/tag/v0.26.1)

### Method 2 — Send payload with Netcat GUI (Modded Warfare)

1. On your PC, run the Netcat GUI (Modded Warfare) to prepare to send the payload.

2. Ensure the USB drive is plugged into the console.

3. Use the Netcat GUI to send the `ps5-app-dumper.elf` payload to the PS5. The payload starts its web interface and reports the address as a notification; open it in a browser to run the dump.

**Downloads:**

* Netcat Gui 1.3: [https://www.sendspace.com/file/v765gd](https://www.sendspace.com/file/v765gd)

### Method 3 — Send payload with socat

1. Put `ps5-app-dumper.elf` in the folder where you'll run `socat` from.

2. With the USB drive plugged in, run the following command on your PC with cmd (replace `<ip>` with the PS5 IP address):

```bash
socat -t 99999999 - TCP:<ip>:9021 < ps5-app-dumper.elf
```

3. The payload will be sent to the PS5 and its log output appears in the socat status window. Open the announced address in a browser to run the dump.

**Download (socat for Windows)**: [https://github.com/tech128/socat-1.7.3.0-windows](https://github.com/tech128/socat-1.7.3.0-windows)

---

## Configuration

`config.ini` lives in `homebrew/ps5-app-dumper/`, together with the list of known disc titles and `logs/` (a general `dumper.log` plus one log per dump) - on a USB drive, or on the console itself under `/data`. **A drive that carries a `config.ini` wins**: it travels with the stick and can be edited on a PC. Without such a drive the console's copy is used, so settings and the access code survive without anything plugged in; *Menu > Settings > Copy to console* puts the drive's settings there as well. The file is rewritten whenever a setting is changed in the web interface. Files that older versions kept in `<drive>/ps5-app-dumper/` or `<drive>/homebrew/` are moved over automatically.

**Where dumps go:** to the selected destination - a USB drive, or *Console storage* (`/data`) when you choose it; it is never picked automatically while a drive is there, and always keeps 10 GB free. Each kind of destination remembers a dump folder of its own (`dump_subdir`, `dump_subdir_console`, both chosen with *Browse*); a new install defaults to `homebrew/ps5-app-dumper/dumps` on both, an existing `config.ini` keeps what it says. Browsing the console's folders needs the access code, browsing a stick does not. Dumps still go to `<drive>/homebrew/` unless `dump_subdir` says otherwise.

### The dumps you have

*Menu > Dumps* lists every dump the payload can find - on each drive and on the console, in the configured folders or anywhere else within a few levels of the root - with its size and state. **Move** takes one to another folder: within a drive at once, between a drive and the console by copying it, comparing the size, and only then removing the original; a stop or an incomplete copy removes the copy instead and leaves the dump where it was. Nothing else runs meanwhile. Dumps on the console are only listed for devices that have entered the access code.

The list can be shown as cards with each dump's own picture, or as a plain list; tapping a dump's path copies it. **Rename** gives every game dump the plain name (`PPSA01325-app0`) or the one with the game's title behind it (`PPSA01325-app0_ASTRO's_PLAYROOM`, what `folder_titles` does for new dumps); DLC keep their names, and a dump ShadowMount runs a game from is left alone. **Delete** removes a dump for good after a dialog that names it, its folder and its size; like Move it only ever touches a folder that is a dump (our info file next to it, or `sce_sys` / `eboot.bin` inside), never while something is running, and never a folder a game is being played from.

> ShadowMount looks for games on its scan paths (`homebrew` among them, searched in depth) and redirects an installed title to a dump it finds there - the title then shows **MOUNT**, runs from the dump instead of its package, and cannot be dumped again. Moving the dump out of its reach is the way out; the payload then removes the link that points at the old place. While ShadowMount is running it links whatever it still finds anew, so the Dumps page says when it is and offers **Stop ShadowMount** (two presses). That only ends the process - start it again the way you usually do.

### Existing and unfinished dumps

Every dump leaves a small `<folder>.dump-info.json` next to its folder: the title, the settings it was made with, and whether it was finished. With that the payload never mixes two dumps in one folder:

* a dump that was **cut short** is removed before its title is dumped again, and is listed under *Unfinished dumps* in the destination panel, where it can be deleted;
* a **finished** dump is only replaced when you confirm it - the start button asks. A queue runs unattended, so it is told up front: *Existing dumps* in the queue card is **Skip** (the default) or **Replace**, the queued titles that are on the drive already carry a **DUMPED** badge, and starting a queue that replaces dumps asks for confirmation once. `auto_start` always leaves such a title alone;
* a folder **without** an info file - an older dump, or something else - counts as finished and is never deleted unasked.

| Key | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `enable_webui` | `1` | Serve the web interface instead of dumping right away |
| `auto_start` | `0` | Dump the running title right at launch; the web UI comes up as well |
| `web_port` | `8081` | First TCP port tried for the web interface |
| `dump_subdir` | `homebrew/ps5-app-dumper/dumps` | Folder below a drive's mount point that receives the dump |
| `dump_subdir_console` | `homebrew/ps5-app-dumper/dumps` | The same below `/data`, when dumping to the console itself |
| `queue_delay` | `30` | Seconds a queued title gets to load before its dump starts, 5-600 |
| `folder_titles` | `1` | Put the game's title behind its dump folders' names, `PPSA01325-app0_ASTRO's_PLAYROOM`; spaces become `_`, characters a file system may refuse are left out. Dumps named either way are recognised |
| `enable_decrypter` | `1` | Decrypt SELF/SPRX files while dumping |
| `enable_elf2fself` | `0` | Re-sign decrypted executables as FSELF |
| `enable_backport` | `0` | Patch SDK versions down — advanced, may break the dump |
| `ps4_backport_level` | `4` | PS4 SDK target, 1-6 |
| `ps5_backport_level` | `1` | PS5 SDK target, 1-10 |
| `enable_logging` | `1` | Write `logs/dumper.log` and one log per dump in the data folder |
| `split` | `3` | PS4 layout: 0 none, 1 app, 2 patch, 3 both |
| `require_code` | `1` | Other devices need the code from the TV before they may change anything; can only be switched in the console's own browser |
| `access_code`, `access_token` | made up | The six-digit code and what a device keeps after entering it. Delete both lines to lock every device out again and get a new code |

The web UI writes the file; hand edits are picked up on the next start, and a value out of range is pulled into it rather than refused.

---

## Contributing

Contributions are welcome. When opening issues or PRs, please include:

* Steps to reproduce the issue.
* Build logs and console output.
* The PS5 firmware version used during testing and any relevant SDK info.

---

## Builds for testers

A build that should not travel: copy `test-build.mk.example` to
`test-build.mk`, fill in the last day, the firmware and the console ids, and
run `make test-build`. The ELF lands in `dist/` under a name that says what it
is, and on any other console or day it ends with a toast (webhb's
`webhb/testgate.c`). A tester learns their console id from `test-probe.elf`
or from the toast of a build that let them in.

## Credits / Links

* Project reference (This Project is base off pfsmnt): [https://github.com/logic-68/pfsmnt-dumper](https://github.com/logic-68/pfsmnt-dumper)
* Project repository: [https://github.com/EchoStretch/ps5-app-dumper](https://github.com/EchoStretch/ps5-app-dumper)
* PS5 Payload SDK (John Tornblom / pacbrew-repo): [https://github.com/ps5-payload-dev/pacbrew-repo](https://github.com/ps5-payload-dev/pacbrew-repo)
* PS5-SELF-Pager ( By Idlesauce): [https://github.com/idlesauce/ps5-self-pager](https://github.com/idlesauce/ps5-self-pager)
* PS4-App-Dumper ( By Alazif @ Scene-Collective): [https://github.com/Scene-Collective/ps4-app-dumper](https://github.com/Scene-Collective/ps4-app-dumper)

latestRelease.name: PS5 App Dumper 2.00 Beta PS5 App Dumper 2.10 Beta
latestRelease.body:
## Highlights

**DLC**
- Each title shows how many DLC are installed for it, with names and sizes
- Dump DLC on the running game dumps its DLC alone, next to a dump you made before, without copying the game again
- With several DLC you pick which ones; a picked DLC that is there already is replaced
- DLC dumps now carry their metadata (param.json, icon) from the installed package (#29)
- DLC that only unlock content in the game are never mounted by the console and have nothing to dump; the page says so instead of hiding the button

**Titles and dumps**
- A DUMPED badge on every title that is dumped somewhere, UNFINISHED for one that was cut short
- New dump folders carry the app title: `PPSA01325-app0_ASTRO's_PLAYROOM` (setting `folder_titles`, on by default)
- Rename on the Dumps page switches every dump to names with or without the title
- Tap a dump's path to copy it, and the Dumps list fits a phone

**Queue**
- Up to 64 titles instead of 16

**Fixes**
- Titles stuck at 99 %  were held as installing for good and could not be dumped
- The UNFINISHED badge was drawn far too big

## Notes
- Dumps made with 2.00 or earlier keep their names and are still recognised. Use Rename on the Dumps page if you want the titles on them too.
- A dump ShadowMount runs a game from is not renamed, because the link points at its folder.

## Thanks
Thanks to @MangoScango for #29, which completes the DLC dumps with their metadata.

## For developers
Built on [webhb](https://github.com/slopmaster33/webhb) 0.4.1. If its download does not work, `webhb-0.4.1.tar.gz` is attached; build with `WEBHB_TARBALL=webhb-0.4.1.tar.gz make`.

repos.name: ps5-60FPS
repos.readme:
fps60

Unlock 60 FPS in PS4 and PS5 games on a jailbroken PS5, with one switch per game.

![fps60 on a TV: the Games tab](docs/fps60-games-tv.png) fps60 is a payload for a jailbroken PS5. It looks at the games you have installed, finds the ones that have a known 60 FPS patch for your exact game version, and lets you switch those patches on from a page on the console's own browser (or your phone). When you start a patched game, fps60 writes the patch into the game's memory as it loads. Your game files are never changed. > The screenshots in this README come from a test run with sample games on a > PC, so the page looks exactly as it does on the console. ## Contents - [What you need](#what-you-need) - [Quick start](#quick-start) - [Tested games](#tested-games) - [Using fps60](#using-fps60) - [How it works](#how-it-works) - [Files on the console](#files-on-the-console) - [Limits and safety](#limits-and-safety) - [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting) - [Versions and releases](#versions-and-releases) - [Building from source](#building-from-source) - [Credits](#credits) ## What you need - A PS5 that is jailbroken and running an **ELF loader** on port `9021`. Firmware up to 13.60 works with the Relapse exploit, which provides one. - A way to send a payload: Payload Manager, the exploit's payload menu, or a computer on the same network (`socat` or `make test`). - Optional: [Payload Manager](https://github.com/itsPLK/ps5-payload-manager), to start fps60 automatically after each jailbreak. ## Quick start 1. **Download `fps60.elf`** from the [latest release](https://github.com/eladharels/ps5-60fps/releases/latest) (or the zip, which also has this README and the changelog). 2. **Send it to the console** after jailbreaking: ```bash socat -t 99999999 - TCP::9021 < fps60.elf ``` or pick it in Payload Manager. The console shows *"fps60 v1.0.0 running: http://<ps5-ip>:8060"*. 3. **Open fps60.** On the home screen, go to **Media** and open the **fps60** tile. It opens the page in the console's browser. On a phone or computer on the same network, open `http://:8060` instead. 4. **Switch on a patch** for a game marked *Matches your version*. 5. **Start the game.** A notification says *"<game>: 60 FPS enabled"*. fps60 keeps running until the console restarts or goes into rest mode. Your switches are saved, so after a reboot you only need to send `fps60.elf` again. To skip even that, add `fps60.elf` to Payload Manager's autoload list. ## Tested games These patches have been confirmed working on a real PS5. They show a **Tested on PS5** label on the Games tab, and the **Tested on PS5** filter lists only them. | Game | Patch | Game version | Notes | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Gravity Rush 2 | 60 FPS | 01.11 | | | The Order: 1886 | 60 FPS Unlock | 01.02 | The patch author notes softlocks in chapters 6 and 9 during quick-time events: switch the patch off to get past them. | The other patches come from the community and should work the same way, but haven't been tried with fps60 yet. If you test one, open an issue with the game, its version and the result, so it can be added here. ## Using fps60 ### Games Every installed game with a frame-rate patch is listed with its title ID, whether it's a PS4 or PS5 game, and the installed version. Each patch has a switch and a label: - **Matches your version:** the patch is made for the version you have installed. You can switch it on. - **Tested on PS5:** confirmed working on a real console (see [Tested games](#tested-games)). - **Needs version X:** the patch exists, but for another game version. Update (or downgrade) the game to use it. - **Not supported by fps60:** the patch uses a feature fps60 doesn't implement. - **Game running:** the game is running now and the patch is on. The author and the patch notes are shown under each patch. Read them: some patches have side effects, such as a cutscene you need to switch the patch off for. - **Search** filters by name or title ID. - **Tested on PS5** shows only tested patches; **All installed games** shows games without a patch too. - **Rescan** reads the installed games again (after installing or updating a game). - **Activity** lists what was applied, and why a patch failed. Switching a patch **on** while the game is running applies it right away. Some games only read their frame-rate setting at startup, so restart the game if nothing changes. Switching a patch **off** takes effect the next time the game starts. The same page works on a phone or computer on your network, at `http://:8060`.
### Logs ![fps60 Logs tab](docs/fps60-logs-tv.png) Every step fps60 takes is logged: - which metadata files it read for each game - when a game starts and exits - where each patch line was written, and which bytes were there before - every error You can filter by level or text, **Copy** or **Download** the log, and **Diagnose** writes every running process and its loaded modules to the log. That shows how a game looks to fps60 if it isn't being detected. While you're on another tab, a red number on **Logs** counts new errors. ### Settings ![fps60 Settings tab](docs/fps60-settings-tv.png) - **Home screen tile:** remove or reinstall the **fps60** tile. If you remove it, fps60 doesn't put it back on its next start. - **Rescan installed games.** - **Stop fps60.** Patches already applied stay in running games. - **About:** the address to open on a phone, the build, and where fps60 keeps its files. ### Updating and stopping - **Update:** send the new `fps60.elf`. It asks the running copy to stop and takes its place, and you get *"fps60 restarted"*. - **Stop:** use **Stop** in Settings, or kill `fps60.elf` in Payload Manager's process list (fps60 names its process `fps60.elf` so it shows up there). ## How it works ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph build["At build time"] repo["Community patches
(GoldHEN XML)"] --> conv["tools/build_patchdb.py
keeps 60 FPS patches"] conv --> db[("patch database
built into fps60.elf")] end subgraph console["On the PS5"] meta["/user/appmeta
param.sfo / param.json"] --> games["installed games
+ versions"] db --> match{"patch for this
title + version?"} games --> match match --> page["web page :8060
switches"] page --> enabled[("/data/fps60/enabled.txt")] watch["watcher, every 100 ms"] --> proc["game process starts"] enabled --> watch proc --> load["wait for its executable
(eboot.bin) to load"] load --> write["resolve every address,
then write the patch
into game memory"] end ``` **There's no system-wide 30 FPS setting.** Every game limits its own frame rate, so every unlock is a hand-made patch for one version of one game. fps60 uses the community patches from [illusion0001/PS4-PS5-Game-Patch](https://github.com/illusion0001/PS4-PS5-Game-Patch). 1. **Patch database.** At build time `tools/build_patchdb.py` keeps only the frame-rate unlocks (about 160) and converts them into a compact format. All value encoding happens there: little-endian integers, floats, UTF-8 and UTF-16 strings, byte patterns with wildcards. The result is built into `fps60.elf`. 2. **Installed games.** fps60 reads each game's metadata, `param.sfo` for PS4 games and `param.json` for PS5 games, from `/user/appmeta`, `/system_data/priv/appmeta` and a few fallback folders. That gives the title ID, name and installed version. 3. **Finding the running game.** A watcher checks the running processes 10 times a second. It identifies games by their title ID and, as a fallback, asks the system which game is in the foreground. That second method is what makes PS4 games running on the PS5 work. 4. **Applying a patch.** When a game with an enabled patch starts, fps60 waits for its executable to load and finds its base address. - It computes every address first: fixed addresses relative to the game's image base, or a search of the game's code for a byte pattern. - Only when all of them are found does it write, so a patch is applied completely or not at all. - Bundles with several executables, such as the Ezio Collection, get each part as its executable loads. - A running game is patched once. Switching a patch off and on doesn't write it again. 5. **The page and the tile.** fps60 serves its page on port `8060`. The home screen tile is a small media app whose link opens `http://127.0.0.1:8060/` in the console's browser. ## Files on the console | Path | What it is | | --- | --- | | `/data/fps60/enabled.txt` | The patches you switched on (one `TITLEIDpatch name` per line) | | `/data/fps60/fps60.log` | The log of the current run (`fps60.log.1` is the previous run) | | `/data/fps60/patches.db` | Optional: a newer patch database to use instead of the built-in one | | `/data/fps60/no-tile` | Present if you removed the home screen tile | | `/user/app/FPSU00060` | The home screen tile | To update the patch list without rebuilding fps60, copy a newer `build/patches.db` to `/data/fps60/patches.db` and send fps60 again. ## Limits and safety - **Coverage.** About 160 patches, almost all for PS4 games running on the PS5. Very few native PS5 games have one. - **Exact versions.** A patch only works on the game version it was made for. - **Side effects.** Some games behave oddly at 60 FPS (physics or timers tied to the frame rate, or stutter when the GPU can't keep up). Read the patch notes. - **Offline only.** Changing a game's memory during online play can get an account flagged. - **Your network.** The page and the ELF loader are reachable by anything on your home network. Don't forward their ports to the internet. ## Troubleshooting | Problem | What to do | | --- | --- | | No games are listed | Open **Logs**: each scanned folder and metadata file is listed. Send the log to whoever helps you. | | Patch shows **Failed** | The Activity line and the log say why: another game version, a pattern that wasn't found, or a write that failed. | | Nothing happens when the game starts | Check that the log shows *game started*. If not, press **Diagnose** and look for the game's process. | | The tile isn't on the home screen | In **Settings**, press **Install tile**, then filter the log for `tile`. | | *"port 8060 is busy"* | Another program uses port 8060, or the running fps60 didn't stop. Restart the console. | | The tile opens an error page | fps60 isn't running. Send `fps60.elf` again (or add it to Payload Manager's autoload). | ## Versions and releases Every version is published on the [Releases page](https://github.com/eladharels/ps5-60fps/releases) with: - `fps60.elf`, ready to send to the console - `fps60-vX.Y.Z.zip`, which holds the same ELF plus this README and the changelog What changed in each version is in [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md) and in each release's notes. The running version is shown in the start notification and under Settings > About. Version numbers follow [semantic versioning](https://semver.org): - **X:** goes up for changes that break your setup. - **Y:** goes up for new features. - **Z:** goes up for fixes. Publishing a new version (for maintainers): 1. In a pull request, put the new number in `VERSION` and add a `## [X.Y.Z] - date` section at the top of `CHANGELOG.md`. 2. Merge it into `main`. 3. The *release* workflow then: - runs the tests - builds with the pinned SDK (v0.44) - creates the tag `vX.Y.Z` - publishes the release with the changelog section as its notes It skips versions that already have a release. You can also start it by hand from Actions > release > Run workflow. ## Building from source ```bash sudo apt-get install make clang-18 lld-18 llvm-18 wget unzip zip python3 git socat wget https://github.com/ps5-payload-dev/sdk/releases/download/v0.44/ps5-payload-sdk.zip sudo unzip -d /opt ps5-payload-sdk.zip export PS5_PAYLOAD_SDK=/opt/ps5-payload-sdk LLVM_CONFIG=/usr/bin/llvm-config-18 make # fps60.elf make check # host tests: no SDK or console needed make dist # build/fps60-vX.Y.Z.zip make test PS5_HOST= # send fps60.elf and stream its log ``` The first `make` clones the patch repository into `build/patch-repo`. Set `PATCH_REPO=` to use an existing checkout. ### Tests `make check` runs on a normal Linux PC with AddressSanitizer and UBSan: - the converter's encoding of every patch value type - a parse of the real patch database - metadata parsing, including damaged files - pattern scans across chunk boundaries - the watcher against a fake game process: apply on start, re-apply after a restart, bundles, and no second write after a switch is turned off and on - the web routes, settings file and log ### CI GitHub Actions builds `fps60.elf`, runs the tests and uploads the `fps60` artifact on every push and pull request. An optional deploy job sends the build to your console. It needs a self-hosted runner on your home network, since GitHub's cloud runners can't reach the console. Configure it with these repository variables: | Variable | Default | Meaning | | --- | --- | --- | | `PS5_HOST` | unset: deploy skipped | Console IP | | `PS5_PORT` | `9021` | ELF loader port | | `PS5_RUNNER` | `ubuntu-24.04` | Runner label for the deploy job | The repository is public, so before adding a self-hosted runner, set Settings > Actions > General > *Require approval for all external contributors*. ### Layout | Folder | Contents | | --- | --- | | `fps60/` | Game scanning (`titles.c`), patch database (`patchdb.c`), patcher (`patcher.c`), watcher and state (`app.c`), console-specific code (`platform_ps5.c`), the page (`ui.html`) and the icon (`assets/`) | | `common/` | Shared payload framework: web server, log, startup/replace/stop (`service.c`), notifications and home screen tile (`sys_ps5.c`), Logs and Settings tabs (`ui/`) | | `tools/` | `build_patchdb.py` (patch converter) and `embed.py` (builds the page, patches and icon into the ELF) | | `.github/workflows/` | `build.yml` (tests and builds every push), `release.yml` (publishes a release for a version tag) | | `tests/` | Host tests | ## Credits - Patches: the authors credited on each patch, collected in [illusion0001/PS4-PS5-Game-Patch](https://github.com/illusion0001/PS4-PS5-Game-Patch) (GoldHEN patch format). - [ps5-payload-dev/sdk](https://github.com/ps5-payload-dev/sdk), the PS5 payload SDK. - The home screen tile uses the approach introduced by John Törnblom's ftpsrv and used by Payload Manager. Sister project: [NetDis](https://github.com/eladharels/ps5-netdis) shows every network port in use on the console.
